issues.issue: The notice states terrorism insurance is 'made available' under the Act, while the same disclosure states the premium attributable to terrorism coverage is $-0- (c010). A court could be asked whether terrorism coverage was in fact purchased.

The definition strings together certification, violence, damage-location and coercive-purpose elements with semicolons and a single 'and', leaving unclear whether all elements are independently required or merely descriptive of the Secretary's certification.

A zero terrorism premium sits against the disclosure in c005 that the policy 'makes available' terrorism insurance with no terrorism exclusion or sublimit. The two could be read as inconsistent about whether the peril is covered.

This recital-like notice describes Executive Liability, EPL and Fiduciary coverage sections, none of which appear in Item 3 Coverage Summary (c020), which lists only General Terms, Crime and Special Coverage. A court could be asked what, if anything, it operates on.
It describes claims-made triggers for coverage sections not purchased under Item 3 (c020), and cannot be squared with the Crime Coverage Section's discovery-based trigger in Exclusion 19 (c115).

The extended reporting period is described only for claims-made sections not included in Item 3 Coverage Summary (c020); it has no counterpart in the Crime section's 60-day post-termination discovery rule (c115).

This Declarations legend describes claims-made coverage sections and defense-costs erosion, yet the only coverage purchased per Item 3 (c020) is Crime/Special Coverage, which has no 'Defense Costs' or 'Claim' mechanism. Its application to this policy is uncertain.
The policy period runs 'To 42:01 A.M.', an impossible time and a plain mechanical error for 12:01 A.M. The expiry moment is therefore not stated correctly on the face of the Declarations.
'SPECIAL COVERAGE' is listed as a purchased coverage with no accompanying definition or coverage section text in the instrument.

Item 3 lists a 'SPECIAL COVERAGE' section, but the Schedule of Forms attaches a Kidnap/Ransom & Extortion Coverage Section instead, and no Special Coverage section appears. The two cannot be reconciled on the face of the policy.

Item 4 designates prior policy number 8212-1392, the same number as the present policy, which Subsection 12 (c047) then terminates as of inception. A court could be asked which instrument is terminated.

Worldwide territory sits against the Compliance With Applicable Trade Sanction Laws endorsement (c058), which withdraws coverage wherever sanctions laws prohibit it. The reach of the worldwide grant is therefore qualified elsewhere.

This priority rule is the instrument's own conflict-resolution tool, and its operation is tested by the several endorsements that amend the same Crime provisions (c149 and c156 both rewrite Exclusion 19). Its ordering of endorsements against coverage-section text is not spelled out.

'Claim' is left to the applicable coverage section, but the Crime Coverage Section's Definitions (Subsection 11) contain no definition of Claim, while the notice provisions (c031) and the Late Notice endorsement (c050) turn on that term. The definition points to a meaning that does not exist for the only coverage purchased.

Notice here is keyed to a 'Claim', but the Crime section conditions coverage on notice of Discovery of loss within ninety days (c136), and defines no Claim at all. Which notice regime governs a crime loss is left unresolved.

This excuse for late notice sits against Subsection 27 of the Crime section (c136), which makes notice within ninety days of Discovery an express condition precedent to coverage. The two set different consequences for the same failure.

The conversion date here (judgment final, settlement agreed, loss due) differs from the Crime section's rule fixing the rate on the day the loss is Discovered (c139), though the opening words 'except as otherwise provided' may harmonise them.
'Full compliance with all the terms of this policy' as a condition precedent is undefined in scope, leaving open whether any breach, however immaterial, bars suit.

Paragraph (f) directs the reader to 'paragraph (g) of this Subsection 11', but no paragraph (g) is lettered in the text; the sub-paragraph lettering (c), (d), (e), (f) is also detached from the text it introduces. The cross-reference cannot be followed as written.
'Customary short rates' is not defined anywhere in the policy and supplies no ascertainable method of computing the refund.

This terminates prior Company bonds at inception, while Subsection 24 Liability for Prior Losses (c125-c127) preserves coverage for losses sustained under those prior bonds; the Conversion endorsement then deletes Subsection 24 altogether.

This endorsement makes late notice fatal only where the Company is prejudiced, while Subsection 27 of the Crime section (c136) makes notice within ninety days of Discovery a condition precedent without any prejudice requirement. The endorsement also speaks only of a 'Claim', a term the Crime section never defines.
